section.title: The Covenant Cut
section.sectionRationale: After the rescue of Lot and the meeting with Melchizedek, Abram is left with a promise but no child. Here God binds Himself by oath to the childless man, and Abram's bare trust is counted as righteousness. This is the theological heart of the Abraham story.
section.thesis: God answers Abram's fear and doubt not with proof he can grasp but with His own word and His own oath; Abram believes, and God credits it to him as righteousness, then cuts a covenant He alone will keep.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the promise of a son and Abram's faith counted as righteousness; the promise of the land questioned; and the covenant ceremony where God alone passes between the pieces.

units.label: The word, the shield, and the reward

verses.text: After these events, the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: “Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your {{shield|shield}}, your very great reward.”
But Abram replied, “O Lord GOD, what can You give me, since I remain childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?”
Abram continued, “Behold, You have given me no offspring, so a servant in my household will be my heir.”
Then the word of the LORD came to Abram, saying, “This one will not be your heir, but one who comes from your own body will be your heir.”
And the LORD took him outside and said, “Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able.” Then He told him, “So shall your offspring be.”
Abram {{believe|believed}} the LORD, and it was credited to him as {{righteousness|righteousness}}.
The LORD also told him, “I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess.”
But Abram replied, “Lord GOD, how can I know that I will possess it?”
And the LORD said to him, “Bring Me a heifer, a goat, and a ram, each three years old, along with a turtledove and a young pigeon.”
So Abram brought all these to Him, split each of them down the middle, and laid the halves opposite each other. The birds, however, he did not cut in half.
And the birds of prey descended on the carcasses, but Abram drove them away.

units.label: The darkness and the word of things to come

verses.text: As the sun was setting, Abram fell into a deep sleep, and suddenly great terror and darkness overwhelmed him.
Then the LORD said to Abram, “Know for certain that your descendants will be strangers in a land that is not their own, and they will be enslaved and mistreated four hundred years.
But I will judge the nation they serve as slaves, and afterward they will depart with many possessions.
You, however, will go to your fathers in peace and be buried at a ripe old age.
In the fourth generation your descendants will return here, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete.”

units.label: God alone passes between the pieces

verses.text: When the sun had set and darkness had fallen, behold, a smoking firepot and a flaming torch appeared and passed between the halves of the carcasses.
On that day the LORD made a {{covenant|covenant}} with Abram, saying, “To your descendants I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great River Euphrates,
the land of the Kenites, Kenizzites, Kadmonites,
Hittites, Perizzites, Rephaites,
Amorites, Canaanites, Girgashites, and Jebusites.”

shield.gloss: A shield, that which protects and covers. God does not merely give Abram a shield; He says I am your shield. The same root lies behind the reward language, for God Himself, not the plunder Abram had just refused, is his defense and his wealth.

believe.gloss: To trust, to rely on, to regard as firm and sure. Our word amen comes from this root. Abram is not achieving anything; he is leaning his whole weight on what God has said. This is the faith that receives, not earns.

righteousness.gloss: Righteousness, a right standing before God. It was credited or reckoned to Abram, an accounting term for something placed to his account. Paul builds his whole doctrine of justification by faith on this verse, Romans 4:3.

covenant.gloss: A binding covenant, often ratified by cutting animals in two. The idiom to cut a covenant pictures the parties saying, let this be done to me if I break faith. Here God alone passes through, taking the whole obligation on Himself.

basic.context: Abram has a promise but still no child, and he is afraid. God comes to him in a vision and answers the two great questions hanging over him: will he have a son, and will his family have a land. The key question the chapter presses is simple: how does a person get right with God?
basic.hermeneutics: This is real history told with care, and one verse in it, verse 6, becomes a foundation for the whole New Testament. The main thing to see is that Abram is counted righteous before he does anything, simply by trusting God's promise. The debate is over what that crediting means, but the plain point is that righteousness comes by faith.
basic.originalLanguages: God calls Himself Abram's shield, the word for the cover that protects a soldier. Abram believed, from the root that gives us amen, meaning he leaned his weight on God's word. That faith was credited, an accounting word, to him as righteousness, a right standing with God.
basic.typology: The covenant is cut by dividing animals, and God alone, pictured as a smoking firepot and flaming torch, passes between the pieces. He takes on Himself the whole penalty for breaking the covenant. That points to the cross, where God in Christ bears the curse His people deserved.
basic.christ: Paul quotes verse 6 to show that we are justified the same way Abram was, by faith, not by works, Romans 4. And the God who alone walks the bloody path foreshadows Jesus, who alone dies to keep a covenant we could never keep.
basic.god: God is a shield to the fearful, a rewarder who gives Himself, and a covenant keeper who binds Himself by oath. He stoops to a doubting man's how can I know and answers not with a rebuke but with a solemn promise.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 4 and Galatians 3 make this chapter the charter of justification by faith. Hebrews 6 speaks of God confirming His promise with an oath. Acts 7 recalls the four hundred years of affliction foretold here.
basic.oneStory: This is where the gospel of grace is written into the story of Abraham. God promises, Abram believes, and God counts him righteous, then swears an oath He alone will keep. The whole line runs to Christ, the true offspring, and to all who share Abram's faith.

context.literary:
The chapter opens with a link and a new kind of language. 'After these events' ties it to Genesis 14: Abram has just defeated four kings and refused the reward the king of Sodom offered. Now 'the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision,' the formula the prophets later use for the arrival of God's word. Genesis will call Abraham a prophet in Genesis 20:7, and this is the first scene in which he receives the word in a prophet's way.

The chapter is built in two parallel panels. Each opens with God's self declaration: 'I am your shield,' verse 1, and 'I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur,' verse 7. Each continues with Abram's honest question: 'what can You give me?' verse 2, and 'how can I know?' verse 8. Each ends with a divine answer that goes beyond words, the stars in verse 5 and the covenant ceremony in verses 9 to 21. The first panel concerns the heir, the second the land, the two promises that Abram still holds without any sign of fulfilment.

At the centre of the first panel stands verse 6, a narrator's comment rather than part of the dialogue. The story pauses to tell the reader how God regarded Abram's response.

The second panel is darker. Time moves from the starry night of verse 5 to a setting sun in verse 12 and full darkness in verse 17, and the scene moves from promise to terror to fire. The prophecy of verses 13 to 16 interrupts the ceremony and tells Abram the cost before the covenant is sealed: four hundred years of affliction. Then the smoking firepot and flaming torch pass between the pieces, and the chapter closes with a list of ten peoples, longer than the usual lists of six or seven such as Deuteronomy 7:1, whose land is promised to Abram's seed. The promise is sealed before it is fulfilled.
context.historical:
Abram's complaint in verses 2 and 3 reflects a known ancient practice. A childless man could designate a trusted household servant as his heir, so that the estate would not be lost. The Hebrew of verse 2 is difficult, but Eliezer of Damascus is clearly the steward in line to inherit. God's answer rules out adoption as the fulfilment of the promise: the heir will come 'from your own body.'

The covenant rite of verses 9 to 11 draws on a practice attested in the Old Testament itself. In Jeremiah 34:18-20 the leaders of Judah 'cut in two' a calf and 'passed between its pieces' when they made a covenant, and God threatens to treat covenant breakers 'like the calf.' Passing between divided animals was a self curse: may I become like these if I break my word. Similar rites of slaughtering an animal to seal a treaty are known from the wider ancient Near East. The shock of Genesis 15 is not the rite but who walks the path.

The animals are exactly those Israel would later bring as offerings: heifer, goat, ram, turtledove and young pigeon, the full range of the later sacrificial system, compare Leviticus 1:10, 5:7 and Numbers 19:2. For the first readers, the scene looked like a sacrifice as well as an oath.

Israel heard verses 13 to 16 as their own history foretold. They had been 'strangers in a land that is not their own,' enslaved and afflicted, Exodus 1:11-12, and had left with silver and gold, Exodus 12:35-36. Exodus 12:40-41 gives the stay as 430 years; Genesis rounds it to four hundred, as Stephen does in Acts 7:6. The 'fourth generation' fits the counting of generations in Exodus 6:16-20, from Levi to Moses. The boundaries 'from the river of Egypt to the great River Euphrates' match the reach of Solomon's rule in 1 Kings 4:21. The smoke and fire recall what Israel saw at the exodus and Sinai, Exodus 13:21 and 19:18.
context.canonical:
Genesis 15:6 is one of the most quoted verses of the Old Testament in the New. The BSB footnote lists four citations: Romans 4:3, Romans 4:22, Galatians 3:6 and James 2:23. Genesis 15:5 is cited in Romans 4:18, and verse 14 in Acts 7:6-7.

Within the Old Testament the chapter's language resurfaces in several places. Psalm 106:31 says of Phinehas, 'It was credited to him as righteousness for endless generations,' the same phrase used of Abram. Nehemiah's great prayer recalls that God 'found his heart faithful' and 'made a covenant with him to give the land,' Nehemiah 9:8, echoing both verse 6 and verse 18. God's shield language returns throughout the Psalms, 'You, O LORD, are a shield around me,' Psalm 3:3, and 'Do not fear' becomes a refrain in Isaiah, Isaiah 41:10.

The covenant was remembered as an oath. Exodus 2:24 says God 'remembered His covenant with Abraham' when Israel groaned in Egypt, and Joseph's last words look to 'the land He promised on oath to Abraham,' Genesis 50:24. When Joshua's generation entered Canaan, the narrator could say, 'Not one of all the LORD's good promises to the house of Israel had failed,' Joshua 21:45.

The New Testament takes up both halves of the chapter. Paul uses verse 6 to argue that justification is by faith, not works, and that Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised, Romans 4:9-11, since Genesis 17, where circumcision is given, comes at least thirteen years later, Genesis 16:16 and 17:1. Galatians 3:17 argues that the covenant ratified here cannot be annulled by the law that came 430 years afterward. James 2:21-23 reads verse 6 as 'fulfilled' when Abraham offered Isaac. Zechariah's song rejoices that God has remembered 'the oath He swore to our father Abraham,' Luke 1:73, and Hebrews 6:13-18 makes that oath the anchor of Christian hope.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to know how their father stood before God and on what basis the promises rested. The chapter shows a man who has obeyed, fought and refused the world's reward, and who is now afraid and still childless. The first hearers were to see that Abram is not reckoned righteous for the victories of chapter 14. The narrator places his verdict, verse 6, in response to Abram believing a promise with nothing yet to show for it.

The second aim is to show where the certainty of the promises lies. Abram asks, 'how can I know?' God does not give him a sign he can inspect. He gives an oath enacted in fire, and He alone passes between the pieces. Israel was to understand that the land they entered and the nation they had become rested finally on God's self binding commitment, not on their own faithfulness.

Third, Moses wanted his people to understand their own history as part of God's plan. The years of slavery in Egypt were not a sign that God had forgotten. They had been foretold to Abram, along with the judgment on Egypt, the exodus with possessions and the return in the fourth generation. The delay was also moral: God would not dispossess the Amorites until their iniquity was complete, verse 16. Israel was to see that God's timing involves both mercy to the nations and justice on them.

Finally, Abram's honest questions, 'what can You give me?' and 'how can I know?', are not rebuked. The first hearers were meant to learn that faith can ask and still believe.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The covenant ceremony is a unique event. Believers are not told to split animals or seek visions, and the specific promises of land and a son belong to Abram and his line. Nor does the chapter teach that every believer will receive a prophecy of their future.

Yet the New Testament explicitly generalises one line. Paul says the words 'it was credited to him' 'were written not only for Abraham, but also for us, to whom righteousness will be credited,' Romans 4:23-24. So verse 6, though it describes one man's experience, prescribes the way every person is accounted righteous before God: by believing the God who promises and raises the dead.

The rest applies by analogy. God's word to Abram, 'Do not be afraid,' is not a promise of a son to every reader, but it reveals a God who meets the fears of His people with Himself. Abram's questions show that honest doubt spoken to God is not unbelief, and his waiting shows that promises may be certain long before they are visible.

debates.question: What does it mean that faith was credited to Abram as righteousness?

views.label: A righteousness reckoned to him, not his own
views.case: The verb chashab is used of counting something to a person's account, and Paul reads it this way, contrasting what is 'credited as a gift' with wages earned, Romans 4:4-5, and linking it with the blessedness of the one to whom God 'credits righteousness apart from works,' Romans 4:6. On this view God declares Abram right with Him on the basis of a righteousness received by faith. This was the Reformers' reading.

views.label: Faith itself counted as a righteous response
views.case: Some note that Psalm 106:31 uses the same phrase of Phinehas's zealous act, and read Genesis 15:6 as God regarding Abram's trust itself as the right and fitting response to His word, within a relationship of covenant loyalty.

views.label: The beginning of a righteousness later completed
views.case: Others, drawing on James 2:21-23, see verse 6 as the start of a life of faith that is 'perfected' in obedience, so that the crediting and Abraham's later offering of Isaac belong together.

debates.bearing: Paul's use of the verse is decisive for Christian reading: the crediting is a gift to one who 'does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the wicked,' Romans 4:5. James does not contradict this; he shows that the faith credited in Genesis 15 is the living faith that obeys in Genesis 22.

debates.question: Why does God alone pass between the pieces?

views.label: God takes the whole obligation and curse on Himself
views.case: In the rite of Jeremiah 34:18-20 both parties walked between the pieces and invoked death on themselves if they broke faith. Here Abram is asleep, and only the fire representing God passes through. God binds Himself unilaterally, so the covenant's fulfilment depends on Him alone.

views.label: A royal grant rather than a mutual treaty
views.case: Some compare the scene to ancient grants in which a king bestowed land on a loyal servant by oath. On this reading the point is that the land is a gift sworn by the giver, not a contract requiring terms from the receiver, though Abram's obligations appear later, Genesis 17:1.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that the promise rests on God's oath. The self curse view adds a sombre depth that the New Testament makes explicit: God keeps His covenant by bearing its curse Himself in Christ, Galatians 3:13-14.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 plays on the previous chapter. God says, 'I am your magen,' shield, and the consonants echo Melchizedek's blessing in Genesis 14:20, 'God Most High, who has delivered (miggen) your enemies.' The God who handed Abram his enemies will now shield him from their reprisals. The 'reward' is sakhar, a word normally used for wages or hire, as when Laban tells Jacob, 'Name your wages,' Genesis 30:28, and Jacob speaks of 'my wages,' Genesis 30:32. Abram has just refused Sodom's reward; God offers a better one. The Hebrew can be read as 'your reward will be very great' or 'I am... your very great reward,' and the BSB takes the second, making God Himself the reward. Paul's contrast between wages and gift in Romans 4:4 lands on a chapter that begins with this word.

Abram addresses God as Adonai YHWH, 'Lord GOD,' in verses 2 and 8, joining the title master to the covenant name. It is the language of a servant who knows to whom he is speaking.

Verse 6 turns on two verbs. 'Believed' is he'emin, the causative stem of aman, whose basic idea is to be firm or reliable; the related amen means 'surely' or 'so be it.' With the preposition be it means to trust in or rely on a person. The form is unusual: instead of the ordinary narrative tense it uses a perfect with 'and,' which some grammarians take to describe a settled, continuing attitude rather than a single moment. Abram's faith is not a flash of assent but a stance.

'Credited' is chashab, to think, reckon or count. It is used in the sacrificial law of an offering being 'credited' or not to the worshipper, Leviticus 7:18, and of a Levite's tithe being 'reckoned' to him as grain from the threshing floor, Numbers 18:27. It is the verb in Psalm 32:2, 'whose iniquity the LORD does not count against him,' which Paul pairs with Genesis 15:6 in Romans 4:6-8. 'Righteousness' is tsedaqah, conformity to a right standard, and in covenant contexts a right standing with God.

Verse 18 uses the standard idiom for making a covenant, karat berit, literally to cut a covenant, and the ceremony enacts the phrase. Abram's 'deep sleep' in verse 12 is tardemah, the same word used when God put Adam to sleep to form the woman, Genesis 2:21, and of the sleep 'from the LORD' that fell on Saul's camp, 1 Samuel 26:12. It is a sleep God sends, in which God acts and the man does nothing.

The 'smoking firepot' is tannur, an oven or furnace, and the 'flaming torch' is lappid. Smoke and torch fire together recall Sinai, where the mountain smoked 'like the smoke of a furnace,' Exodus 19:18, and the people saw the 'lightning,' lappidim in Hebrew, Exodus 20:18.

typology.type: God alone passing between the pieces, verse 17
typology.fulfillment: In the covenant rite each party invoked death on himself if he broke faith, Jeremiah 34:18-20. Here only God passes through, as if to say that He will bear the curse of covenant breaking. The New Testament shows what that meant: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' so that 'the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles,' Galatians 3:13-14. The type falls short only in that the animals merely pictured death; at the cross God in Christ actually bore it.

typology.type: Abram credited with righteousness through faith, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: Abram believed a promise about a son he could not yet see and was counted righteous. Paul says the words 'were written not only for Abraham, but also for us,' who believe 'in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead,' Romans 4:23-25. The escalation lies in the object of faith. Abram trusted God to bring life from a man 'as good as dead,' Hebrews 11:12; believers trust God who has already brought Jesus back from death, and are credited with 'the righteousness of God' in Him, 2 Corinthians 5:21.

typology.type: The smoking firepot and flaming torch
typology.fulfillment: God's presence appears as smoke and fire in the dark, as it later does in the pillar of cloud and fire that led Israel out of Egypt, Exodus 13:21, and on smoking Sinai, Exodus 19:18. In Christ that presence comes near without consuming. John says 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and that the one and only Son has made the Father known, John 1:18. The fire that passed between the pieces in the night is the same holy God who, in Jesus, walked among His people and went Himself into the darkness of the cross, Matthew 27:45-46.

typology.type: The affliction in a foreign land and the exodus with possessions, verses 13 and 14
typology.fulfillment: Abram's seed would be strangers and slaves, then brought out by God's judgment with great possessions. The exodus became Israel's defining picture of redemption. The New Testament presents Christ's work as a greater exodus: He came to 'free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death,' Hebrews 2:15, and on the mount of transfiguration He speaks of 'His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem,' Luke 9:31, where the Greek word for departure is exodos. Egypt's bondage was political; the bondage Christ breaks is sin and death.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through verse 6. Paul builds his argument on it: 'Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,' Romans 4:3. He stresses that Abraham was counted righteous 'apart from works,' Romans 4:6, and before circumcision, Romans 4:10. Then he draws the line straight to Christ: the words were written 'also for us, to whom righteousness will be credited, for us who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead,' Romans 4:24. Abram's faith was in a God who could give life to a dead body; ours is in the God who raised Jesus. The object has come into focus, but the way of being made right is the same.

Where does the righteousness credited to believers come from? Paul answers in 2 Corinthians 5:21: 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.' The crediting of Genesis 15:6 finds its ground in Christ, whose righteousness is counted to those who trust Him, Philippians 3:9.

It leads to Christ through the covenant rite. God alone passed between the pieces, taking on Himself the curse of a broken covenant. In Galatians 3 Paul ties the promise to Abraham, the curse of the law and the cross together: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13, so that the blessing of Abraham would reach the Gentiles. On the night before He died, Jesus spoke of 'the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20. The covenant God swore by Himself in the dark is kept by God the Son in the darkness at noon, Mark 15:33.

It leads to Christ as the promised heir. The whole chapter hangs on the question of who will inherit. Paul says the promises were spoken to Abraham 'and to your seed,' meaning Christ, Galatians 3:16, and that the covenant ratified then cannot be set aside by the law, Galatians 3:17.

Finally, the chapter's opening word, 'I am your shield, your very great reward,' finds its deepest answer in Christ, in whom God gives not only gifts but Himself. 'He who did not spare His own Son,' Paul asks, 'how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things?' Romans 8:32.
study.god:
The chapter opens with God answering fear before Abram voices it. 'Do not be afraid' comes first, then 'I am your shield.' God knows what His servant feels after a war with four kings and before a future with no heir. His self description is personal: not 'I will give you a shield' but 'I am your shield,' not 'I will pay you' but 'I am your very great reward.' The chief gift God gives is Himself.

God is patient with honest questions. Abram's 'what can You give me?' and 'how can I know?' are met not with rebuke but with a starry sky and a covenant. The God of Genesis 15 is not offended by a servant who asks how, as long as the question is brought to Him.

He is the God who counts. The verb of verse 6 shows God as the One who reckons, who decides how a person stands before Him. His verdict is sovereign and gracious: He credits righteousness to a man who has only believed. This is not God ignoring justice; the rest of Scripture shows He will provide the ground for it in Christ, Romans 3:26, 'so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus.'

He is the God who binds Himself. In the covenant rite He alone walks between the pieces, putting His own name and life, as it were, under the curse. Hebrews says that since God 'had no one greater to swear by, He swore by Himself,' Hebrews 6:13. His faithfulness does not depend on Abram, who is asleep, but on His own character.

He is also the Lord of history and the Judge of the nations. He tells Abram in advance about four hundred years of affliction, the judgment of Egypt, and the return. He says the Amorites' iniquity 'is not yet complete,' verse 16. God does not act before justice is ripe; He is patient even with the nations who will lose the land, and He judges them only when their sin is full, Leviticus 18:24-25.

For worship, the chapter invites believers to rest where Abram rested. The promise is secured by God's oath, not by our strength. Our part is to believe, and to count the stars.

crossReferences.note: Paul quotes Genesis 15:6 to show that Abraham was not justified by works. Wages are owed, but the one who 'does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the wicked' has faith credited as righteousness. He then pairs the verse with Psalm 32:1-2, the blessing of forgiveness.

Abraham's faith was credited to him before his circumcision, which came years later in Genesis 17. Circumcision was a seal of a righteousness already given by faith, so Abraham is father both of uncircumcised believers and of circumcised ones who walk in his faith.

Paul quotes Genesis 15:5, 'So shall your offspring be,' and says Abraham 'in hope believed' against all hope. The words 'it was credited to him' were written also for those who believe in the God who raised Jesus from the dead.

Paul cites Genesis 15:6 to show that 'those who have faith are sons of Abraham.' The Scripture 'foretold the gospel to Abraham' in the promise that all nations would be blessed in him, so Gentile believers share Abraham's blessing by the same faith.

A covenant previously ratified by God cannot be annulled by the law that came 430 years later. Paul takes the covenant of Genesis 15 as an unconditional promise to Abraham and his Seed, Christ, which the Sinai law could not add conditions to.

James quotes Genesis 15:6 and says it was 'fulfilled' when Abraham offered Isaac, his faith 'perfected by what he did.' He shows that the faith credited in Genesis 15 is a living faith that later obeys. James and Paul address different errors about the same text.

The one Old Testament passage that describes the rite of Genesis 15. Judah's leaders cut a calf in two and passed between its pieces, and God warns that covenant breakers will become like that calf. It shows why God's passing alone between the pieces in 15:17 is so striking.

Since God had no one greater to swear by, He swore by Himself. His promise and His oath are 'two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie,' giving believers strong encouragement. The self binding oath of Genesis 15 becomes an anchor for Christian hope.

Of Phinehas the psalm says, 'It was credited to him as righteousness for endless generations to come,' the same phrase used of Abram in Genesis 15:6. The parallel shows how the phrase could describe God's approval of a faithful response, and why the meaning of 15:6 is discussed.

Stephen summarises Genesis 15:13-14: Abraham's descendants would be enslaved four hundred years, God would punish the nation that enslaved them, and they would come out and worship. The BSB notes that he cites verse 14. The prophecy is presented as fulfilled history.

When Israel groaned under slavery, 'God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham.' The covenant sealed in Genesis 15 is what moves God to act at the exodus, keeping the promise of verse 14 that He would judge the nation they served.

Christ became a curse for us, so that the blessing promised to Abraham might come to the Gentiles. The covenant in which God alone passed between the pieces, taking the curse upon Himself, is fulfilled at the cross, where God in Christ bears the curse His people deserved.

study.oneStory:
Since Genesis 3 the question has hung over humanity: how can sinful people be right with a holy God? The early chapters show people trying their own way. Cain brings his offering and is not accepted, Genesis 4:5, and the builders of Babel try to make a name for themselves. Genesis 15 gives the first clear answer. A man is counted righteous not by his achievements, not even the victories of chapter 14, but by believing God's promise.

The chapter also answers a second question from Genesis 12. God had promised Abram a seed and a land, but years have passed with neither. Here God puts the promises under oath and shows that they rest on Him alone. He also sketches the path ahead: slavery in Egypt, judgment on the oppressor, an exodus and a return. The rest of the Pentateuch unfolds exactly that path, and Joshua closes with the testimony that 'not one of all the LORD's good promises' had failed, Joshua 21:45.

Yet the land was lost again in exile, and Israel's own covenant breaking showed that a people who could not keep covenant needed a God who would bear its curse. The prophets promised a new covenant, Jeremiah 31:31-34, grounded not in Israel's faithfulness but in God's forgiveness.

The story reaches its centre at the cross. There the God who passed alone through the pieces bears the curse Himself in the person of His Son, Galatians 3:13, and there the righteousness credited to Abram by faith is secured for all who believe, Romans 4:24-25. Jesus names the cup 'the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20, and the blessing of Abraham reaches the nations.

The story ends where the stars promised. The offspring beyond counting becomes 'a multitude too large to count, from every nation,' Revelation 7:9, standing before the throne. The land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates becomes a new earth, and those who, like Abram, believed God will live in His presence, their shield and very great reward, forever.

quiz.q: Why was Abram counted righteous in this chapter?

options.text: Because he believed the LORD's promise, and it was credited to him as righteousness.
options.note: Verse 6 grounds righteousness in faith, not achievement.

options.text: Because he offered the animals God commanded.
options.note: The sacrifice belongs to the covenant scene, but righteousness is credited before it, through faith.

options.text: Because he had rescued Lot and refused the king's plunder.
options.note: Those acts precede this chapter, but the text credits righteousness to his faith, not his deeds.

options.text: Because he had earned it by a lifetime of obedience.
options.note: The point of verse 6 is that righteousness came by believing, not by earning.

quiz.q: What is the significance of God alone passing between the divided animals?

options.text: God binds Himself by oath, taking the whole obligation of the covenant on Himself.
options.note: In the ceremony the one who passes through pledges his life; God takes that on alone.

options.text: It shows the covenant depended on both parties keeping their word.
options.note: Normally both parties passed through, but here only God does, which is the striking point.

options.text: It was simply the customary way to seal any agreement.
options.note: The form was customary, but God walking alone is the surprising, meaningful departure.

options.text: It meant Abram had to guarantee the covenant himself.
options.note: Abram is asleep; the whole weight falls on God, not on him.

quiz.q: How does God describe Himself to the fearful Abram in verse 1?

options.text: As Abram's shield and his very great reward.
options.note: God offers protection and Himself as the reward.

options.text: As the God who will make him wealthy and famous.
options.note: God does promise blessing, but here He offers Himself as the reward, not merely riches.

options.text: As a distant judge who demands performance.
options.note: God comes near with comfort, not distant demand.

options.text: As a God who cannot be questioned.
options.note: God welcomes Abram's honest how can I know and answers with an oath.

quiz.q: What did God foretell about Abram's descendants?

options.text: They would be strangers and enslaved in a foreign land, then come out with many possessions.
options.note: This foretells the Egyptian bondage and the exodus.

options.text: They would immediately possess the whole land in Abram's lifetime.
options.note: The land is promised, but only after four generations and much affliction.

options.text: They would never face any hardship.
options.note: God plainly foretells enslavement and mistreatment first.

options.text: They would be abandoned by God in their suffering.
options.note: God promises to judge the oppressor and bring them out.

quiz.q: Why does the New Testament return so often to Genesis 15:6?

options.text: Because it teaches that a person is justified by faith in God's promise, not by works.
options.note: Paul builds justification by faith on this verse, Romans 4 and Galatians 3.

options.text: Because it gives the boundaries of the promised land.
options.note: The boundaries matter, but the New Testament's focus is Abram's faith counted as righteousness.

options.text: Because it records the first animal sacrifice.
options.note: It is not the first sacrifice, and that is not the reason it is cited.

options.text: Because it proves salvation is earned by obedience.
options.note: It proves the opposite: righteousness comes by faith apart from works.

questions: God told Abram, 'Do not be afraid, I am your shield.' What fear are you carrying this week, and what would it mean to let God Himself be your protection?
Abram was counted righteous simply by believing God's promise. Do you tend to think God accepts you because of what you do, or because of what you trust Him to do?
Abram asked honestly, 'How can I know?' Is there a place where you need to bring your real doubts to God rather than hiding them?
God alone walked the path of the covenant, taking the cost on Himself. How does it change your view of God to see Him bind Himself to keep a promise you could never keep?
God gave Himself as Abram's 'very great reward.' What are you tempted to treasure more than God, and what would it look like to find your reward in Him?

translationNotes.note: Your very great reward can also be rendered your reward will be very great; either way the LORD offers Himself, not merely a gift, as Abram's reward.
The verb rendered credited or reckoned is an accounting term; the New Testament reads it as God placing righteousness to the believer's account by faith.
